actionThatDiffers: Instead of cycling five panes to discover who is blocked and answering each as found, the user defers, then clears all pending prompts in one deliberate pass, so one context switch replaces five.
why: Blocked-ness of any single session is on screen in its own pane, and a tmux list-panes + capture-pane loop plus pane activity times yields an adequate approximation of who is waiting; the queue is an ordering over inputs that are individually visible, so rules 2 and 3 cap access at 60. Cross-harness split assumed: needs-input is reliably detectable only for Claude (briefing says so for Cargento), elsewhere it is inferred from pane text, hence dependsOnDetector true.

actionThatDiffers: User stops keeping a browser tab open to poll hosted runs; a cloud run that finished or wedged gets picked up in the same sweep as local panes instead of being forgotten until the next manual check.
why: Briefing does not cover cloud or hosted sessions at all, so this is first-principles: local sessions are in panes (visible), cloud runs live behind a web UI that is one or two clicks away but a different place entirely. Two places, no correlation needed, so mid-band access. Impact is convenience plus occasional catch, not loss prevention; the decision it changes is weak.

actionThatDiffers: When quota is nearly gone the user stops the one session actually consuming it and lets the other four keep running, instead of stopping everything or guessing wrong and losing the wrong session's work.
why: Briefing is explicit: quota is shown as a current figure and no harness attributes consumption to a particular session. A pane sweep shows which sessions look busy, which is only a crude proxy for burn (context size matters more than visible chatter), so it is not an adequate approximation. Attribution rests on a token-rate heuristic rather than billing data, so dependsOnDetector true.

actionThatDiffers: With a per-run dollar figure the user routes the next instance of that task to a cheaper model or a different subscription; without it they keep running everything on the expensive default. Weak because on a flat subscription the cost is already sunk when the number arrives.
why: Nothing in any harness shows cost; the briefing only credits a current quota figure. Token counts do sit in session files on disk, so it is derivable by script, but that is correlating across sessions plus a pricing table, which a normal user will not do reliably. Impact held near the rule-1 ceiling: the differing action is real but retrospective and infrequent, and depends on a pricing/attribution heuristic.

actionThatDiffers: Triage order changes: the user answers the session blocked 40 minutes ago before the one blocked 40 seconds ago, so the longest-idle agent stops burning wall-clock first.
why: Blocked-or-not is visible in each pane, and last-activity time is available from tmux pane fields or transcript mtimes, so a six-line loop gives an adequate approximation of duration. Duration plus sort is an arithmetic composite over individually visible inputs, so capped at 60 by rule 3. Shipped state given the same scrutiny as unbuilt items (rule 6). Split assumed: needs-input detection is Claude-reliable, inferred elsewhere.

actionThatDiffers: Before kicking off a large refactor the user waits for the window reset or moves it to a different subscription, instead of starting and hitting the wall mid-task with half-applied edits.
why: Briefing: no harness projects a burn rate forward, and none estimates how long a turn will take. Both inputs to an overrun forecast are absent, so nothing computes this anywhere and no pane sweep approximates it. Rule 4 applies: access is genuinely high but the value rests entirely on a forecast heuristic being right, which also holds impact below the top band.

actionThatDiffers: The user hands four related sessions to a workflow with defined stages and gates instead of hand-carrying context between four panes; they stop being the message bus.
why: Kind is action (rule 5): commissioning a workflow is something the user does, and doing it today is roughly one prompt to an existing commission surface, so 21-40. Briefing does not cover workflow commissioning, hence low confidence. The suggestion half - noticing that these four sessions are one project - is a grouping heuristic, so dependsOnDetector true. Impact is a real behaviour change but rare and heavyweight, not a recurring decision.

actionThatDiffers: Notifications stop interrupting a deep-work block; the user reads them at the end of the block instead of at arrival. Weak delta because the agents then sit idle for the whole window, so it trades one loss for another.
why: Kind is action - flipping a suppression window. The OS already has a one-click Do Not Disturb that covers desktop popups, and the briefing notes no harness delivers notifications off the machine anyway, so there is little left to suppress. Briefing does not cover quiet hours as a feature, hence low confidence. Rule 5 floors an existing-toggle action in the 21-40 band.

actionThatDiffers: The user answers a retrospective question - what did this session do on Tuesday, how often was I interrupted - by querying instead of re-reading transcripts. No decision follows from the history itself; the decisions belong to the items it enables, and crediting those here would double-count them.
why: Briefing states plainly that no harness retains queryable history across sessions. Raw transcripts do sit on disk, so the substrate exists, but assembling a queryable record across sessions and across time is exactly the correlation a normal user will not do. dependsOnDetector false: this is recording data that exists, not inferring a number. Impact held at 48 per rule 1 - an enabler with no concrete action of its own.
